rv.q: With their northern English accents and wild beards of grey, they are an excellent match, capturing the irascibility and interdependence of a couple who no longer know what day it is, still less what happened yesterday.
A stunning revival of one of the most important works in the history of theatre.
It finds freshness and humour in the darkest absurdity, and celebrates forgiveness and love even in the bleakest of settings.

The genius here is that from Costigan and Kelly, their generosity of spirit and the combined efforts of a theatre that understands equity, the traditions that hamstring many, are here used as a secure platform to spring forward.

Spring is in the air, and it’s time, once again, to pick up the dusty mid-20th century gem that is Samuel Beckett’s great 1953 play Waiting For Godot ; to turn it towards the light, and see what brilliant facets and new aspects it will reveal this time.
It’s an entertaining production which is, at times, gratifying but which really struggles to find the space between ‘tragi’ and ‘comedy’.
In a world full of uncertainty, Matthew Kelly and George Costigan’s performance of Waiting for Godot still resonates profoundly today.

cn.t: Dominic Hill's production earns widespread acclaim as a masterclass in staging Beckett's absurdist classic. Critics praise the stark post-apocalyptic design and the bleakly funny performances, particularly the compelling double act at its center.
